dedupe_keys.name: gao 25 106253 climate risks to hazardous waste treatment storage and disposal facilities

description: This Government Accountability Office review asks how exposed the United States' hazardous waste treatment, storage and disposal facilities are to natural hazards that climate change may worsen, and whether the Environmental Protection Agency requires or encourages them to manage that risk. GAO overlaid federal data on the more than 1,000 facilities regulated under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act with federal data on flooding, wildfire, storm surge and sea level rise, reviewed agency documents and interviewed EPA headquarters and regional staff, state agencies and stakeholder groups. The producer is the U.S. Government Accountability Office (report GAO-25-106253, November 2024). Coverage is national, with facility data as of July 2023. More than 700 facilities, about 68 percent, lie in areas with at least one of the hazards: more than 500 in flood areas, nearly 400 in wildfire areas, nearly 200 in storm surge zones and over 100 in sea level rise areas; GAO found that EPA had clarified authorities for permits but not for inspections and enforcement, and made nine recommendations that EPA accepted. The report is free to read online as HTML, with regional maps and an appendix listing the federal hazard data used. Caveats: exposure is by location only, without facility-level design or protection, and the facility list is not published as a table in the report. Simulation uses: prioritising hazardous waste sites in flood and wildfire scenarios and modelling release risks for emergency response. Related records: the EPA Norfolk study (case_study-norfolk-waste-infrastructure-climate-vulnerability) examines municipal waste facilities in one city.

outcomes: Federal hazard data show more than 700 of over 1,000 hazardous waste treatment, storage and disposal facilities (about 68 percent) sit in areas exposed to flooding, wildfire, storm surge or sea level rise (more than 500 flood, nearly 400 wildfire, nearly 200 storm surge, over 100 sea level rise); GAO made nine recommendations, including training, technical assistance and assessing regulations, and EPA agreed.
